claims.text: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles constitute a high-entropy alloy configuration.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a uniform lattice structure at room temperature.
In situ aberration-corrected TEM equipped with a heating stage can investigate the thermal behavior of these nanoparticles at atomic resolution.
The heating experiment is conducted in the vacuum environment of the TEM.
Temperature is gradually ramped without exceeding the melting or sintering threshold.
Heating will produce only subtle atomic rearrangements, minimal defect formation, or very slight diffusional changes.
High-resolution TEM images and diffraction patterns can reveal the proposed atomic rearrangements, defects, diffusion-related changes, and phase changes.
High configurational entropy in nearly equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles reduces the driving force for phase transitions at elevated temperature.
High configurational entropy reduces atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
Suppression of phase transitions and atomic diffusion maintains the structural integrity of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during heating.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will undergo limited atomic-scale rearrangement or phase change under high-temperature conditions below melting or sintering.
Nanoparticles with lower configurational entropy will exhibit more pronounced structural changes under comparable heating.
High-entropy or compositionally complex alloys are of interest for elevated-temperature materials.
The room-temperature atomic structure and lattice parameters provide a baseline for comparison with heated states.
Subtle transient phases or short-lived rearrangements may occur below the temporal or spatial resolution of TEM.
Significant rearrangement, phase transformation, or defect aggregation below the expected thermal threshold would falsify the predicted minimal-change behavior.
